    Seaborn for Exploratory Data Analysis

    Learn Seaborn the way analysts use it: one real dataset, one business question at a time. You will go from a one-line chart to multi-panel grids and presentation-ready visuals, and every chart ends with a finding a manager could act on.

    01Basic

    Why Seaborn?

    You can already draw charts with Matplotlib and df.plot(). Seaborn adds a statistical layer on top, built for the fast question-and-answer loop of exploratory analysis.

    What

    Seaborn is a statistical visualization library built on Matplotlib. It works directly with pandas DataFrames: you name the columns, and Seaborn handles grouping, aggregation, color, legends and uncertainty.

    Why

    In EDA you make dozens of quick charts to find patterns. When each chart is one line, your time goes into questions instead of plotting code. Its defaults, like confidence intervals and grouped colors, are designed for comparing groups.

    How

    import seaborn as sns, then call a function such as sns.histplot(data=df, x="fare"). Seaborn draws on Matplotlib axes, so everything you know about plt still works for titles, limits and saving.

    JobBest first toolWhy
    Quick look at one columndf["fare"].plot(kind="hist") or sns.histplot()Both are one line; Seaborn adds KDE, hue and better bins
    Compare a number across groupsSeabornAggregates raw rows per group and shows uncertainty
    See a pattern for every segmentSeaborn figure-level functionscol= and row= make small multiples automatically
    A custom layout or annotationMatplotlib (on top of Seaborn)Fine control over every element
    02Basic

    The case and the data

    You are a junior analyst at a New York City taxi operator. Before anyone builds a dashboard, the operations director wants you to explore one month of trip records and report what you find.

    #Business questionWhere we answer it
    Q1Where does fare revenue come from: which boroughs, which taxi type?3, 7, 12
    Q2What does a typical trip look like: fare, distance, duration?6, 14
    Q3When is demand highest: hour of day, day of week?4, 7, 11
    Q4What drives the fare?8, 9, 10
    Q5What drives tips, which are part of driver income?7, 9
    What

    Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the first pass through a dataset to learn its shape, quality and patterns before modeling or reporting.

    Why

    Charts catch problems that summary tables hide: recording quirks, skew, spikes, groups that behave differently. Decisions built on unexplored data inherit its errors.

    How

    Start from business questions, audit the data, then move from one variable to two to many. Write down each finding and the next question it raises.

    Set up the notebook

    Run this cell once at the top of your notebook. sns.set_theme() switches every later chart to Seaborn's look; the dictionary maps each taxi type to its real color so charts are easy to read.

    Load and audit

    Seaborn ships with practice datasets. load_dataset() downloads one and returns a regular pandas DataFrame (it needs an internet connection the first time). Each row is one taxi trip.

    ColumnMeaningType for plotting
    pickup, dropoffStart and end timestampsdatetime
    passengersRiders entered by the drivernumeric (small integer)
    distanceTrip length in milesnumeric

    paymentcredit card or cashcategorical

    Audit before you plot. Check the size and missing values, then the summary statistics.

    Analyst's notebookAudit
    Finding
    44 trips have no payment type and 26 to 45 have no pickup or dropoff zone (92 rows in total). The minimum distance is 0.00 miles, and passengers has a minimum of 0, which is a driver entry habit, not a real trip with nobody in it.
    Decision
    Drop rows with missing values, drop trips that never moved, and keep March 2019 only (one trip starts on February 28). That removes 125 rows, 1.9% of the data: too few to change the picture, and it keeps group comparisons clean.
    Note
    Keep passengers as is. It is not central to our questions, and we will see later that it has almost no relationship with fare.
    Why .copy()?

    Filtering returns a slice of the original DataFrame. Adding columns to a slice triggers pandas' SettingWithCopyWarning. .copy() makes taxis an independent table, so the next cell runs without warnings.

    Feature engineering

    Charts can only use columns that exist. These five derived columns let us ask time and tipping questions later. DAYS and BOROUGHS are lists we will pass to order= so categories appear in a sensible order.

    Version note

    pandas 3 shows text columns as str; pandas 2 shows object. Every cell in this tutorial works the same in both, and with Seaborn 0.13 or newer.

    03Basic

    Your first chart, three ways

    Question Q1: what is the average fare by pickup borough, split by taxi type? Draw it with the tools you know, then with Seaborn, and count what you had to do yourself.

    You compute the means, reshape them, position every bar, then build the ticks and legend by hand.

    Shorter, but you still aggregate and pivot first. .plot() draws whatever table you give it.

    Seaborn starts from the raw rows. It grouped 6,308 trips, computed each mean, drew 95% confidence intervals (the black lines), built the legend and labeled the axes.

    Two differences are worth noticing. Seaborn lists categories in the order they first appear in the data, while pandas sorts them alphabetically; you will control this with order=. Seaborn also softens bar colors slightly by default (saturation=0.75).

    Analyst's notebookQ1
    Question
    Do average fares differ by borough and taxi type?
    Finding
    In Queens, yellow taxis average $33.38 per trip while green taxis average $13.47. In the other boroughs the two fleets are within a few dollars of each other.
    So what
    A likely explanation: Queens is home to JFK and LaGuardia airports, and yellow taxis serve airport trips while green taxis serve neighborhoods. That is a hypothesis, not yet a finding.
    Next question
    Can we see airport trips in the fare distribution? (Section 6 and Section 10 test this.)
    04Basic

    The grammar of a Seaborn call

    Almost every Seaborn function speaks the same language: a DataFrame plus a mapping from column names to visual channels.

    What

    data= takes a DataFrame. Column names go to channels: position (x, y), color (hue), dot size (size), marker shape (style) and panels (col, row).

    Why

    Thinking in mappings lets you add a dimension to a chart by adding one argument. The vocabulary is shared, so learning one function teaches you most of the others.

    How

    Pick the question, pick the columns, assign each column to a channel. Step through the lab below and watch one scatterplot grow from two variables to five.

    Live lab · add one channel at a time500 random trips, so individual dots stay readable

    Two channels. Fare rises steadily with distance. A handful of trips sit on a flat line at $52 no matter how far they go.

    Color adds payment type. Cash and card trips sit on the same price line, so payment method does not change what the meter charges.

    Dot size adds the tip. Every orange cash dot is the smallest size: cash tips are recorded as $0. That is a data question, and Section 7 checks it.

    Panels add taxi type. The flat $52 trips appear only in yellow taxis. Note the function changed from scatterplot to relplot: panels need a figure-level function (Section 5).

    Seaborn wants long-form (tidy) data

    What

    Long-form data has one row per observation and one column per variable. Wide-form data spreads one variable across several columns, like a pivot table.

    Why

    Seaborn maps column names to channels. If "taxi color" is stored as two column headers instead of one column, there is no column to give to hue=.

    How

    Use df.melt() to turn wide into long. Keep identifier columns with id_vars=; name the new columns with var_name= and value_name=.

    Analyst's notebookQ3
    Question
    When during the day is demand highest?
    Finding
    Trips bottom out around 5 AM and climb steeply until 8 AM. Yellow demand peaks at 6 to 7 PM. Green taxis follow a much flatter daily curve.
    So what
    Scheduling more yellow drivers from late afternoon into the evening matches demand; overnight coverage can be thin.
    Next question
    Does the pattern differ by day of the week? (Section 11 draws a day-by-hour heatmap.)
    05Basic

    Two kinds of functions

    Seaborn's functions come in families. Knowing which family a function belongs to tells you what it can do and how to size and arrange it.

    What

    Axes-level functions draw on one Matplotlib Axes (histplot, boxplot, scatterplot). Figure-level functions build a whole figure and can split it into panels (displot, catplot, relplot).

    Why

    Mixing them up causes the most common Seaborn errors. Axes-level functions fit layouts you build with plt.subplots(); figure-level functions make small multiples with col= and row=.

    How

    Composing a dashboard? Use axes-level with ax=. One chart per group? Use figure-level with col=, sized by height= and aspect= instead of figsize.

    Function family explorerSelect any function

    Axes-level: you place each plot

    Figure-level: Seaborn makes the panels

    06Intermediate

    Distributions: the shape of one variable

    Question Q2: what does a typical trip cost? Before comparing anything, look at how a single variable is spread.

    What

    Distribution plots show how the values of one variable are spread: center, spread, skew, gaps, spikes and outliers. histplot, kdeplot, ecdfplot for numbers; countplot for categories.

    Why

    Averages hide shape. Pricing, staffing or forecasting from a mean goes wrong when the data is skewed or has two peaks. EDA always starts by looking at each key variable alone.

    How

    Start with sns.histplot(data=df, x=col). Tune bins or binwidth, add kde=True, and compare groups with hue= plus stat="percent" and common_norm=False.

    Live lab · bins and bandwidthReal fares from all 6,308 trips, drawn in your browser

    Try this

    Drag bins down to 14. The spike at $52 merges into its neighbors and disappears. Now turn on the KDE and set bw_adjust to 0.3, then 2.0. A smoothing choice can create or erase a pattern, so try more than one setting before you report a shape.

    Compare distributions across groups

    There are 5,357 yellow trips and only 951 green ones. Plain counts would make the green histogram tiny. stat="percent" with common_norm=False scales each group to 100% so the shapes can be compared; element="step" draws outlines so the overlap stays visible.

    ECDF: what share of trips are below a value?

    An empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF) rises from 0 to 1. Read a fare on the x-axis, go up to the curve, and read the share of trips at or below it. No bins, no smoothing choices.

    Categories: count them

    Analyst's notebookQ2
    Question
    What does a typical trip look like?
    Finding
    Fares are strongly right-skewed: the median trip costs $9.50 but the mean is $12.89. 57% of yellow and 54% of green trips cost $10 or less. A sharp spike at exactly $52 appears only in yellow taxis (123 trips). Manhattan accounts for 83% of pickups.
    So what
    Use the median when describing a typical trip. The $52 spike matches New York's 2019 flat fare between Manhattan and JFK Airport, so airport trips behave like a separate product.
    Next question
    Which boroughs do the $52 trips start in? (Section 10 answers with a FacetGrid.)
    histplot parameterWhat it controlsUse it when
    bins, binwidthNumber or width of barsDefault bins hide or exaggerate detail
    kde=TrueAdds a smooth density curveYou want the overall shape at a glance
    stat"count", "percent", "density", "probability"Comparing groups of different sizes
    common_norm=FalseNormalizes each hue group on its ownAlways pair with a non-count stat when comparing groups
    element"bars", "step", "poly"Overlapping groups

    07Intermediate

    Comparing categories

    Most business questions are comparisons: which region, which channel, which day. Categorical plots put a group on one axis and a number on the other.

    What

    Three kinds: plots that show every point (stripplot, swarmplot), plots that summarize a distribution (boxplot, violinplot), and plots that show one estimate per group (barplot, pointplot, countplot).

    Why

    The plot type decides whether you see the full spread or only an average. A bar of averages can hide skew, outliers and two-peaked groups.

    How

    Spread: box or violin. One number per group with uncertainty: bar or point. Set category order with order= and hue_order=, and choose the statistic with estimator=.

    Boxplot: five numbers and the outliers

    Anatomy of a boxManhattan pickups, real values

    Violin: when the box hides two peaks

    The Queens box looks like one wide group. The violin shows two bulges: short local trips around $10 and a second peak near $52. cut=0 stops the curves at the real minimum and maximum, and density_norm="width" gives every violin the same maximum width so shapes are easy to compare.

    Barplot: which statistic does the bar show?

    Each bar is the average fare per trip; the black line is a bootstrapped 95% confidence interval. Queens leads at $24.62 and Manhattan is lowest at $11.07.

    Each bar is the middle trip. Medians sit below the means because fares are right-skewed: Manhattan's median is $8.50 against a mean of $11.07.

    Each bar is total fare revenue. Manhattan brings in $57,744, almost four times Queens, even though its average trip is the cheapest.

    EDA trap

    barplot shows the mean by default, not the total. "Which borough makes the most money?" needs estimator="sum". "Which borough has the most expensive trips?" needs the mean or median. Match the statistic to the question.

    Layering plots: box plus raw points

    Axes-level functions draw on the same Axes when called one after another. Here a light box summarizes tips while a strip plot shows every trip in the 500-trip sample.

    Every cash tip sits exactly at $0. Is that customer behavior or a recording rule? Check the numbers.

    Analyst's notebookQ5
    Finding
    All 1,775 cash trips record a tip of $0.00. The city's trip data only captures tips paid by card; cash tips are not recorded.
    Decision
    Analyze tips with card trips only. Treating cash as "no tip" would understate tips by about a quarter of all trips.
    Lesson
    Before interpreting a pattern, ask how the data was recorded. A chart showed the problem; a groupby confirmed it.

    pointplot shows each group's mean with a confidence interval, connected so you can follow a trend across ordered categories. Card riders tip about 23% to 24% of the fare every day of the week. The intervals overlap heavily, so these small wiggles are noise.

    Read the axis

    Unlike bars, a point plot's y-axis does not start at zero. Here it spans only 22.5% to 25%, which makes a one-point difference look dramatic. Always check the scale before you call a difference large.

    Predict first: which weekday is busiest?

    Make a predictionThen reveal the chart

    Pick the day you think has the most taxi trips.

    EDA trap: exposure

    Friday has the most trips in total (1,086), but March 2019 had five Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays and only four of every other weekday. Per calendar day, Wednesday leads (238 trips) and Friday falls to third (217). Before comparing totals, divide by the opportunity each group had: days, stores, customers or hours.

    08Intermediate

    Relationships and trends

    Question Q4: what drives the fare? Relational plots show how one number changes with another.

    What

    scatterplot draws one dot per observation. lineplot aggregates repeated x values (the mean by default) and connects them, with a confidence band.

    Why

    Pricing, cost and demand questions are relationships. Scatterplots reveal straight-line trends, clusters, business rules (like flat fares) and outliers that one correlation number hides.

    How

    sns.scatterplot(data=df, x=..., y=...) with alpha= for large data. sns.lineplot(data=df, x=..., y=...) for an ordered x such as hour; control the band with errorbar=.

    Live lab · overplottingAll 6,308 trips; drag alpha down

    At alpha 1.0 the short-trip corner is one solid blob: you cannot tell 10 trips from 1,000. Lower alpha so overlapping dots stack up into darker areas.

    Lineplot: a trend with uncertainty

    For each hour, Seaborn averaged every trip's fare and bootstrapped a 95% confidence interval for that average. The band is wide at 5 AM because only 50 trips start in that hour.

    errorbar=ShowsAnswers
    ("ci", 95)95% confidence interval of the mean (default)How precisely do we know the average?
    "sd"Mean plus or minus one standard deviationHow spread out are individual trips?
    ("pi", 50)Middle 50% of the dataWhere do typical trips fall?
    NoneNo bandClean presentation when uncertainty is shown elsewhere
    Analyst's notebookQ4
    Finding
    Fare climbs in a straight line with distance. A horizontal row of trips at $52 between about 10 and 30 miles breaks the line: the flat airport fare. The average fare peaks at 5 AM ($17.06), but only 50 trips start then.
    So what
    Distance explains most of the fare, so a simple rule could estimate fares. Early-morning trips are longer, likely airport runs, but too few to plan around on their own.
    Next question
    How many dollars does each extra mile add? (Section 9 fits the line.)
    09Intermediate

    Regression lines

    A fitted line turns "fare goes up with distance" into a number you can use: dollars per mile.

    What

    regplot and lmplot draw a scatterplot plus a fitted linear regression line and its 95% confidence band.

    Why

    The slope summarizes a relationship in business units, and the points that stray from the line show where the simple rule breaks.

    How

    regplot (axes-level) for one fit; lmplot (figure-level) to fit separately per hue or col. Seaborn draws the fit but does not print coefficients, so use np.polyfit for the numbers.

    Each extra mile adds about $2.74 to the fare, on top of a $4.62 starting point. That is close to New York's 2019 meter: $2.50 when the meter starts, plus $2.50 per mile while moving, plus a time charge in slow traffic. The data recovers the pricing rule, and the time charge explains why the fitted numbers run slightly higher.

    lmplot: one fit per group

    Analyst's notebookQ5
    Finding
    For yellow taxis, card tips rise about 17 cents per extra fare dollar. Green taxis split into two groups: tips that grow with the fare, and a flat band of $0 tips. 46% of green card trips record no tip, against 5% for yellow.
    So what
    One regression line for green taxis would average two different behaviors into a misleading flat line. Before analyzing green-taxi tip income, ask the data owner how those tips are captured.
    Caution
    A regression line describes association in this data, not cause. It also should not be stretched beyond the range of observed trips.
    10Advanced

    Multi-panel grids

    One call, many related plots: a whole-dataset overview, or the same chart repeated for every segment.

    What

    pairplot plots every pair of numeric columns. jointplot shows one pair plus each variable's distribution. FacetGrid repeats any plot for each category.

    Why

    They give an overview in seconds, and small multiples make segment comparisons fair: every panel uses the same axes and the same encoding.

    How

    pairplot(data, vars=, hue=, corner=True); jointplot(kind="scatter" | "hex" | "kde" | "reg"); FacetGrid(data, col=, row=) then .map_dataframe(plot_function, x=...).

    pairplot: everything against everything

    corner=True drops the mirror-image upper half. The diagonal shows each variable's distribution. Distance, duration and fare rise together; the tip row has a floor of orange cash trips at $0, the recording rule from Section 7 showing up again.

    jointplot: one relationship, in depth

    Hexagonal bins count how many trips land in each cell, which solves overplotting without transparency. "bins": "log" puts the color scale on a log scale so thin areas stay visible next to the dense core of 1 to 2 mile trips. The margins show each variable's own histogram, and the $52 band stands out in the right-hand margin.

    FacetGrid: build your own small multiples

    FacetGrid sets up the panels; map_dataframe calls any plotting function once per panel with that panel's rows. sharey=False gives each panel its own y-scale because Manhattan has eight times more trips than Queens.

    Analyst's notebookQ1 + Q2
    Finding
    Queens has the tallest $52 spike of any borough: 79 of its 625 pickups are flat-fare trips. The other 44 flat-fare trips start in Manhattan, heading to JFK.
    So what
    This confirms the Section 3 hypothesis. Yellow-taxi revenue in Queens is airport revenue, and it should be reported as its own line.
    11Advanced

    Heatmaps

    A heatmap colors every cell of a table. Managers already think in grids: day by hour, region by product, metric by metric.

    What

    sns.heatmap() draws a 2-D table as colored cells. Two common inputs: a correlation matrix and a pivot table.

    Why

    A 7-day by 24-hour schedule has 168 numbers. As a table it is unreadable; as a heatmap the busy and quiet periods jump out.

    How

    Build the matrix with pandas (.corr(), pivot_table()), then sns.heatmap(matrix, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap=...). Diverging colors centered at 0 for correlations; sequential colors for counts.

    Correlation matrix

    Distance and fare correlate at 0.96 and duration and fare at 0.90. Passengers correlates with nothing (about 0.00): a New York meter charges per trip, not per rider. center=0 with the diverging "vlag" palette makes positive values red, negative values blue and zero white.

    Correlation is not causation

    A correlation of 0.47 between distance and tip does not mean distance makes people tip. Longer trips cost more, and tips are roughly a percentage of the fare. Look for the mechanism before acting on a correlation.

    Demand by day and hour

    Analyst's notebookQ3
    Finding
    The busiest slot is Thursday at 6 PM (19.25 trips per Thursday in this sample). 3 to 5 AM is nearly empty on weekdays. Saturday's first hours, which are really Friday night, average 7.9 trips per hour against 1.7 on Monday.
    So what
    Weekday evening rush is the core demand window; weekend late nights need far more coverage than weekday late nights.
    Why per day?
    The cell divides counts by the number of each weekday in March (n_days), avoiding the exposure trap from Section 7.
    Going further

    sns.clustermap() draws a heatmap that reorders rows and columns so similar ones sit together. It is useful for finding groups of similar products, stores or customers.

    12Advanced

    Style and storytelling

    Exploration charts are for you. Presentation charts are for decision makers. The same data can be ignored or acted on depending on whether the chart states its point.

    What

    Themes (set_theme, set_style, set_context), palettes (color_palette) and Matplotlib finishing touches: titles, labels, number formats and despine.

    Why

    A busy, unlabeled chart forces the reader to do the analysis. A clear title, readable labels and one highlight color make the finding obvious in five seconds.

    How

    Set a theme once at the top. Pick a palette that matches the data type. Then add an insight title, units, value labels, and remove what does not help.

    Styles

    set_style() changes only the background, grid and frame. set_theme() resets everything (style, context, palette and any rc settings), so use it once at the top. Grids help readers look up values; white and ticks suit charts with value labels.

    Contexts: scale for the audience

    Contexts scale fonts and line widths together by the factor shown on each tab. Use "talk" for slides you present: the chart stays readable from the back of a classroom.

    Palettes: match color to data type

    Palette explorerColors pulled from Seaborn itself

    From exploration to presentation

    Fine for you: it answers your question. A manager has to work out what "fare" in the 60,000 range means and which bar matters.

    The title states the finding. Bars are sorted, values are labeled in dollars, the confidence lines and unneeded frame are gone, and one calm color keeps attention on the message.

    Presentation checklistHow
    Title states the insight, not the variablesax.set(title="Manhattan pickups bring in 71% ...")
    Labels in plain words with unitsax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Total fare, March 2019")
    Sorted categoriesorder=[...]
    Readable numbersax.bar_label(), ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter("${x:,.0f}")
    Less inkerrorbar=None when not needed, sns.despine()
    Legend out of the waysns.move_legend(ax, "upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))

    Save the chart

    Why before plt.show()?

    In a script, plt.show() displays the figure and then clears it, so a later savefig writes a blank image. dpi=200 keeps text sharp in slides, and bbox_inches="tight" trims extra white space.

    13Advanced

    The objects interface

    Since version 0.12, Seaborn includes a second way to build charts: a layered, declarative API in seaborn.objects.

    What

    You build a plot as a chain: so.Plot holds the data and mappings, .add() adds a layer made of a mark (what to draw) and an optional stat (how to transform the data), then .facet(), .scale() and .label() refine it.

    Why

    Separating marks from stats makes complex charts read like a recipe. Layers combine freely, which the classic functions only allow through layering tricks.

    How

    import seaborn.objects as so, then chain methods inside parentheses. In Jupyter, a Plot displays itself; in a script, end the chain with .show().

    so.Plot(taxis, x=, y=)→ .facet(col="color")→ .add(so.Dots())→ .add(so.Line(), so.PolyFit())→ .scale() · .label()

    Data and mappings, then panels, then one layer per mark, then scales and labels.

    Notice color="color" inside the first .add(): a mapping can belong to one layer only. The dots are colored by taxi type while the fitted line stays black. The objects interface also has its own theme, so .theme(sns.axes_style("whitegrid")) matches it to the rest of our charts.

    Classic functionObjects equivalent
    sns.scatterplot(...).add(so.Dots())
    sns.lineplot(...) (mean per x).add(so.Line(), so.Agg())
    sns.barplot(...).add(so.Bar(), so.Agg())
    sns.histplot(...).add(so.Bars(), so.Hist())
    sns.regplot(...) line.add(so.Line(), so.PolyFit(order=1))
    hue="payment"color="payment"
    col="color".facet(col="color")
    Which API should you use?

    The classic functions remain fully supported and are what most tutorials, Stack Overflow answers and colleagues use. Learn them first; reach for seaborn.objects when you want to combine several layers in one chart.

    14Review

    Practice lab

    Four business questions. Write the code in your notebook first, then reveal a solution and compare your interpretation.

    E1

    How long is a typical taxi ride?

    Hint: filter out rides of an hour or more, then use a distribution plot with a 2-minute bin width.

    Interpretation. Most rides take 4 to 12 minutes and the median is 11 minutes. The long right tail means a few long rides pull the average up, so quote the median.

    E2

    Does the average fare change by weekday?

    Hint: a categorical plot with one estimate per group, in calendar order.

    Interpretation. Average fares range only from $12.34 (Sunday) to $13.47 (Wednesday), and the confidence intervals overlap. Weekday does not meaningfully change what a trip costs; it changes how many trips there are.

    E3

    Do card tip percentages differ by borough and taxi type?

    Hint: use the cc DataFrame (card trips), a plot that shows spread, and hue= for taxi type.

    Interpretation. Manhattan yellow-taxi riders tip the most, a median of about 27% of the fare. Green taxis show many 0% tips; in the Bronx, 92% of green card trips record no tip at all. That looks like a data-capture difference worth raising before anyone compares driver earnings.

    E4

    How does traffic change trip duration through the day?

    Hint: an ordered x (hour), an average with uncertainty, one line per taxi type.

    Interpretation. Yellow-taxi trips average about 11 minutes at 2 AM and about 16 minutes at 3 PM, when traffic is heavy. The green line jumps around with wide bands because there are few green trips per hour, so do not read much into its early-morning peaks.

    15Review

    EDA findings report

    This is what you hand the operations director: findings in plain language, each with its evidence and a recommended action.

    1

    Manhattan brings in 71% of fare revenue, even though its trips are the cheapest.

    $57,744 of $81,283 in March fares; average Manhattan trip $11.07 against $24.62 in Queens. Revenue comes from volume, not price.

    ActionProtect Manhattan coverage; treat outer-borough trips as higher-value but low-volume.

    Evidence: barplot with estimator="sum" (Sections 7 and 12)

    2

    Airport flat fares are a separate product.

    123 yellow trips cost exactly $52, the 2019 Manhattan to JFK flat fare. 79 start in Queens, which is why yellow Queens trips average $33.38.

    ActionReport airport trips on their own line; averages that mix them in mislead.

    Evidence: histplot spike, violinplot, FacetGrid (Sections 6, 7, 10)

    3

    Demand peaks on weekday evenings; early mornings are nearly empty.

    Trips peak 5 to 8 PM (Thursday 6 PM is the busiest slot) and bottom out 3 to 5 AM. Weekend late nights are several times busier than weekday late nights.

    ActionAlign driver shifts with the evening peak and weekend nights.

    Evidence: lineplot and day-by-hour heatmap (Sections 4 and 11)

    4

    Midweek days are busiest per day; raw totals say otherwise.

    March 2019 had five Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays. Per calendar day, Wednesday (238 trips) beats Friday (217).

    ActionAlways normalize totals by exposure before ranking periods, stores or regions.

    Evidence: side-by-side barplots (Section 7)

    5

    The fare follows the meter rule.

    Fitted line: fare = 4.62 + 2.74 * distance, close to the 2019 meter rate plus time charges. Distance and fare correlate at 0.96.

    ActionUse the rule as a quick fare estimate, and flag trips far off the line for data checks.

    Evidence: regplot, np.polyfit, correlation heatmap (Sections 9 and 11)

    6

    Tip data is incomplete.

    Cash tips are never recorded ($0 on all 1,775 cash trips), and 46% of green-taxi card trips record no tip compared with 5% for yellow. Card riders tip a steady 23% to 24% of the fare every day of the week.

    ActionAnalyze tips on card trips only and ask the data owner about green-taxi tip capture before reporting driver income.

    Evidence: box plus strip, groupby check, lmplot (Sections 7 and 9)

    Your EDA checklist

    Use this list on every new dataset. Your ticks are saved in this browser.

      16Review

      Key points and pitfalls

      Seaborn is a statistical layer on Matplotlib

      It aggregates raw DataFrame rows for you and returns Matplotlib objects you can still customize.

      data= plus column names

      Map columns to channels: x, y, hue, size, style, col, row. One argument adds one dimension.

      Long-form data

      One row per observation. Convert wide tables with melt().

      Axes-level vs figure-level

      Axes-level takes ax= and fits your layout; figure-level makes panels with col=/row= and sizes with height/aspect.

      Look at shape before averages

      Histograms, KDEs and ECDFs reveal skew, spikes and two-peaked groups. Try several bin and bandwidth settings.

      Bars show the mean by default

      Pick estimator= to match the question: mean, median or sum.

      Respect uncertainty

      Overlapping confidence intervals mean the data cannot separate the groups. Read the axis scale before calling a difference large.

      Normalize by exposure

      Divide totals by days, customers or stores before ranking groups.

      Question surprising patterns

      $0 cash tips were a recording rule, not behavior. Ask how data was captured.

      Present the finding, not the chart

      Insight titles, labeled units, sorted bars, one highlight color, saved at dpi=200.

      Common errors and fixes

      AttributeError: ... got an unexpected keyword argument 'col'

      You passed col= (or row=) to an axes-level function such as scatterplot or histplot. Panels need the figure-level partner: relplot, displot or catplot.

      UserWarning: `displot` is a figure-level function and does not accept the ax= parameter

      The chart appears in a new figure instead of your subplot. Use the axes-level partner inside your layout, for example sns.histplot(data=taxis, x="fare", ax=axes[0]).

      figsize is ignored on my displot / relplot / catplot

      Figure-level functions create their own figure. Size them with height= (inches per panel) and aspect= (width divided by height).

      My bars show averages but I wanted totals

      Add estimator="sum" and usually errorbar=None. For counts of rows, use countplot.

      Categories appear in a strange order

      Seaborn uses the order of first appearance for text columns. Pass order= (and hue_order=) with a list, such as order=DAYS.

      ValueError: Could not interpret value `colour` for `hue`

      The column name is misspelled or does not exist, or your data is wide-form so the variable is spread across column headers. Check df.columns and use melt() if needed.

      The scatterplot is a solid blob

      Lower alpha, plot a sample(), or switch to jointplot(kind="hex") or kdeplot.

      Two charts were drawn on top of each other

      Axes-level functions draw on the current Axes. In a script, call plt.show() or plt.figure() between charts. In Jupyter, put each chart in its own cell.

      The legend covers the data

      sns.move_legend(ax, "upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1)) moves it outside the plot area. For figure-level grids, pass the grid object instead of ax.
